source_title: Zenefits Founder Parker Conrad Resigns After Compliance Failures
company_context: Zenefits, a fast-growing HR/benefits-software startup that sold health insurance brokerage alongside free HR software. Co-founder/CEO Parker Conrad resigned in February 2016 after revelations that the company used unlicensed staff to sell insurance and built a software 'macro' to bypass licensing-course requirements. COO David Sacks became CEO. The company survived but was heavily restructured.
business_type: HR SaaS plus insurance brokerage (venture-backed startup)
company_size_stage: Hyper-growth late-stage startup (had raised at a ~$4.5B valuation in 2015) entering regulatory crisis
geography: United States (HQ San Francisco; multi-state insurance operations)
macro_context: Late-stage VC boom with 'growth at all costs' culture colliding with state insurance-licensing regulation.
outcome_category: 16 - founder/key-person/team failure (compliance-driven CEO exit), resolving toward 3 - severe distress but survival
evidence_summary: Co-founder Parker Conrad, CEO since 2012, resigned in February 2016 after disclosures that Zenefits used unlicensed employees to sell health insurance and that a software macro let staff circumvent pre-licensing study requirements. In Washington state, more than 80% of policies sold through August 2015 were sold by staffers without state brokers' licenses. COO David Sacks took over as CEO and named a former federal prosecutor as chief compliance officer. The company later agreed to a $7 million California fine (half suspended absent future violations), and in 2018 Conrad personally surrendered his California insurance license. The company survived in restructured form.

owner_decision_context: The board/founder faced a compliance crisis in which the company's go-to-market growth engine itself was unlawful; leadership had to decide between defending the founder and restoring regulatory legitimacy.
action_taken: Founder-CEO resigned; COO installed as CEO with a new chief compliance officer; company settled with regulators, repriced its valuation, and restructured operations to operate lawfully.
outcome_evidence: Company survived but was severely distressed: leadership replaced, valuation marked down, $7M California settlement, and the founder's personal insurance license surrendered in 2018.
source_limitations: Secondary journalism; the $7M fine and license surrender are corroborated by California Department of Insurance press materials (insurance.ca.gov) which could not be fetched (403) but appear in primary-domain search results. Valuation figure is from market reporting.
